name: Greyfriars Hall
description: Rising above the Cowgate with a Gothic tower and pointed windows, Greyfriars Hall began life around 1861 as Cowgatehead Church, one of several 19th-century churches built to serve Edinburgh's crowded Old Town parishes. The congregation eventually moved on and the building passed out of religious use, standing empty for years before being restored as part of Virgin Hotels Edinburgh, which opened across three linked historic buildings on the site in 2022. The old nave's vaulted ceiling and stone tracery survive intact inside, now used as an event space seating up to 150, while a new glass-fronted extension - visible right beside the old tower - was built onto the church to house the hotel's modern guest floors.

name: Tomb of John Bayne of Pitcairlie
description: Built into the boundary wall of Greyfriars Kirkyard, this weathered stone mausoleum commemorates John Bayne of Pitcairlie, a writer to the signet (a senior class of Edinburgh lawyer) who died in 1681. Bayne made his name and fortune supervising the building contracts for Charles II's 1670s renovation of Holyrood Palace, working alongside architects Sir William Bruce and Robert Mylne on major Edinburgh projects including Canongate Kirk and the Tron Kirk. His widow, Eupham Aikman, won permission from the Town Council in 1684 to raise this monument in his memory; masons Philip Alisone and Patrick Hunter built it, and James Andersone painted and gilded the carved surface, which still carries a long Latin inscription.
interesting_fact: Carved into the statue's hand is a purse holding the royal signet - a nod to Bayne's own career - while the tomb's sheer opulence reflects a wider shift in the kirkyard after 1660, when burial inside the church itself was outlawed and wealthy Edinburgh families began competing instead to build the grandest possible monument out in the yard.

name: Greyfriars Kirk
description: Standing at the edge of its own kirkyard just off George IV Bridge, Greyfriars Kirk was Edinburgh's first church built after the Reformation, opening on Christmas Day 1620 on land that had belonged to a Franciscan friary until Reformers destroyed it in 1559. A gunpowder explosion in 1718 - stored in the tower during a siege - wrecked much of the structure, and the church was later split into two separate congregations, Old and New Greyfriars, that worshipped side by side until reuniting in 1929. It remains an active Church of Scotland parish today, its plain harled walls and squat tower giving little outward hint of the momentous scene that unfolded just outside its door in 1638.
interesting_fact: The National Covenant - a mass declaration against royal interference in Scottish worship - was laid out on a flat tombstone in the churchyard on 28 February 1638 for signing, and within weeks copies had circulated the country so widely that tens of thousands of Scots had added their names, some reputedly signing in their own blood.

name: Greyfriars Kirkyard
description: Greyfriars Kirkyard has served as one of Edinburgh's main burial grounds since 1562, when Mary Queen of Scots granted the town council land that had previously belonged to a Franciscan friary - the 'grey friars' whose robes gave the site its name. With the Old Town's older kirkyards long full, Greyfriars became the resting place for generations of merchants, lawyers and reformers, and its crowded rows of table tombs, wall monuments and grand mausolea now form one of the richest collections of post-Reformation funerary architecture in Scotland. Notable residents include James Craig, the young architect who won the competition to design Edinburgh's New Town but died in poverty and lies in an unmarked grave here. Just inside the main gate on Candlemaker Row is also the small headstone marking where Bobby, the loyal terrier commemorated by the statue at this leg's end, was buried in 1872.
interesting_fact: By the early 1800s the kirkyard was so tempting a target for body-snatchers supplying the city's anatomy schools that grieving families began fitting heavy iron cages called mortsafes over freshly dug graves - several can still be seen bolted in place near the kirkyard's boundary walls today.

name: Covenanters' Prison
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard (Forrest Road side), Edinburgh EH1 2QL
description: In the southeast corner of Greyfriars Kirkyard, behind a locked iron gate off Candlemaker Row, lies the walled enclosure known as the Covenanters' Prison. After the Covenanter army was crushed at the Battle of Bothwell Bridge in June 1679, around 1,200 prisoners were marched to Edinburgh and held here in the open air for more than four months, each allotted just four ounces of bread a day. Dozens died of exposure and starvation before winter set in; others were tried and executed, escaped, or bought freedom by signing a bond renouncing the Covenant. In November 1679 some 257 survivors, sentenced to transportation to the American colonies, were marched to Leith and put aboard a ship that wrecked off Orkney soon after - nearly all drowned, still shackled below deck.
interesting_fact: The grand mausolea now crowded inside the enclosure mostly date from after 1705, when the ground was formally laid out for burials - meaning almost none of the monuments a visitor sees today existed when the Covenanters were actually confined here in the open air in 1679.

name: The Black Mausoleum
description: Tucked against the southern boundary wall of Greyfriars Kirkyard, this domed classical mausoleum was built for Sir George Mackenzie of Rosehaugh, the King's Advocate who prosecuted the Covenanters imprisoned metres away in 1679 and earned the nickname 'Bloody Mackenzie' for the executions he ordered during the period later known as the Killing Time. Designed by architect James Smith and completed shortly before Mackenzie's death in 1691, its drum-shaped, colonnaded form was unusual for Restoration-era Scotland. Mackenzie was also a founding force behind the Advocates' Library, later absorbed into the National Library of Scotland just up the street.
interesting_fact: Local legend holds that a homeless man sheltering inside the mausoleum in December 1998 fell through a collapsed floor into an underground burial vault full of disturbed remains, triggering the 'Mackenzie Poltergeist' - years of reported scratches, bruises and fainting among visitors that made this one of the most-investigated 'haunted' sites in Britain, and led the kirkyard's keyholder to have the tomb locked and exorcised in 1999. Tour guides and Harry Potter fan sites also point to the mausoleum's poltergeist as a possible inspiration for Hogwarts' own mischievous poltergeist, Peeves - a comparison Rowling has never confirmed and that appears to rest on general atmosphere rather than any documented naming link.

name: Bedlam Theatre
description: A short walk past Greyfriars, this red sandstone Gothic building at the corner of Forrest Road and Bristo Place was built in 1848 as the New North Free Church, designed by Thomas Hamilton, one of the architects behind the Scott Monument and the Royal High School. The congregation left in 1941, and after decades as a University of Edinburgh chaplaincy and storeroom, students converted the deconsecrated church into a theatre in 1980-81, keeping its steep gabled roof and lancet windows intact. Today the Bedlam Theatre is the oldest continuously running student theatre in Britain, staging around forty University of Edinburgh Theatre Company productions a year and packing in up to eight separate Fringe shows a day every August.
interesting_fact: The theatre takes its name not from the church but from the area's earlier history: this stretch of Forrest Road once stood beside Edinburgh's 'Bedlam', a poorhouse and asylum, where the poet Robert Fergusson - a major influence on the young Robert Burns - died in 1774 at just twenty-four.

name: Greyfriars Bobby Statue
address: Corner of George IV Bridge & Candlemaker Row, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ
description: This life-size bronze statue and drinking fountain was sculpted by William Brodie and unveiled in 1873 at the junction of George IV Bridge and Candlemaker Row, opposite the entrance to Greyfriars Kirkyard. It was funded by the English philanthropist Baroness Angela Burdett-Coutts. Standing barely a foot tall, it's said to be the smallest listed structure in Edinburgh.
interesting_fact: Bobby was a small terrier - accounts differ on whether he was a Skye Terrier or a Dandie Dinmont - who belonged to John Gray, a nightwatchman with the Edinburgh City Police. Edinburgh's Lord Provost, Sir William Chambers, was so taken with the story that in 1867 he personally paid for the dog's licence and had him fitted with a collar, now on display in the Museum of Edinburgh.

name: Captain John Porteous's Grave
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ (near the west wall)
description: Buried near the west wall of the original kirkyard on 9 September 1736, this is the grave of Captain John Porteous of the Edinburgh City Guard. After a mob hanged smuggler Andrew Wilson in the Grassmarket on 14 April 1736, Porteous ordered his men to fire into the surrounding crowd, killing six bystanders; he was convicted of murder but reprieved by the Crown. On the night of 7 September 1736 a mob dragged him from the Tolbooth and lynched him from a dyer's pole in the Grassmarket, in what became known as the Porteous Riots.
